query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing trace amount (~0.25–0.5 at.%) of boron into equal-atomic NbMoTaW will enhance room‐temperature ductility by promoting boron segregation at grain boundaries that mitigates crack nucleation, while preserving the single-phase BCC matrix that underpins its high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW in its as-cast single-phase BCC form, noted for excellent mechanical strength at 1600 °C and predicted resistance to irradiation but with very poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a trace dopant of boron (on the order of 0.25–0.5 atomic percent) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Samples should be processed under conditions similar to conventional NbMoTaW fabrication. Mechanical tests will be performed at room temperature to assess ductility and at 1600 °C to verify high-temperature strength. Additionally, irradiation experiments (e.g., Fe-ion irradiation up to several dpa) will be conducted to monitor defect evolution and hardness changes.
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of boron atoms to grain boundaries causing the formation of thin, ductile intergranular films, which reduce boundary embrittlement and crack initiation.
generation.mechanism: Boron atoms, due to their low solubility at BCC lattice sites, preferentially segregate at grain boundaries. This segregation reinforces grain-edge cohesion by reducing stress concentrations and impeding early crack nucleation at room temperature. Since the boron content remains extremely low, it is not expected to form any deleterious secondary phases, thereby preserving the high melting-point, single-phase BCC structure that confers superior high-temperature mechanical performance and supports irradiation tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated NbMoTaW alloy (with <5% room-temperature strain-to-failure), the boron-doped version is predicted to show a marked increase in room-temperature ductility (e.g., ductility rising to >15% strain) while maintaining similar yield strength at 1600 °C and negligible changes in irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy processed under the same conditions without boron addition.
generation.boundary: The boron concentration must be maintained at trace levels (≤0.5 at.%) to avoid formation of brittle boride phases or other precipitates that could undermine both room-temperature ductility and high-temperature performance; processing routes must preserve the overall single-phase BCC structure.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies on RHEAs modified with trace dopants (see PMC9586648::web::002 and PMC6397024::web::002) support the idea that minor dopants can improve room-temperature mechanical response via grain-boundary modifications, and interstitial alloying studies (e.g., PMC5227964::web::011) demonstrate that enhancing ductility by promoting additional deformation mechanisms is possible, it remains uncertain how effectively boron will segregate in NbMoTaW and whether it will disturb the high-temperature phase stability or irradiation resistance. The application of trace boron doping specifically to NbMoTaW is novel and thus calls for focused validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of NbMoTaW alloy samples: one group with 0.25–0.5 at.% boron added under identical processing conditions as the control group (no boron). Characterize both groups using microstructural techniques (TEM, APT) to determine phase purity and verify boron segregation at the grain boundaries. Subject both groups to mechanical testing at room temperature and 1600 °C, and expose samples to controlled irradiation (e.g., Fe-ion irradiation up to a predetermined dpa level).
measurements: Room-temperature tensile or compressive strain-to-failure to assess ductility
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) for microstructure and boron segregation
Fractography to evaluate crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped NbMoTaW samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (i.e., if the strain-to-failure remains close to that of the undoped control, within experimental error, or if high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance is degraded relative to the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.
